## February 29, 1960 — A Monday

Gilbert and Sullivan saw you coming. In their 1879 comic opera *The Pirates of Penzance*, a young man named Frederic discovers that because he was born on February 29, he has technically had only a handful of birthdays despite being in his twenties — and is therefore still legally bound to his pirate apprenticeship. The joke is eighty-one years old and it still applies: you are sixty-six years old in 2026, but the date itself has appeared on a calendar only sixteen times. The pirates would say you're barely a teenager.

---

**An earthquake destroyed a city the night you were born.** In the early hours of February 29, 1960, a tremor struck Agadir, Morocco. The city was largely built of earthen construction, and it offered no resistance. Perhaps a third of the population died within seconds — somewhere between twelve and fifteen thousand people. The disaster made international headlines on the morning of your birth. You arrived into a world that was, on that exact day, absorbing a catastrophe.

**Twenty-one days after your birth, sixty-nine people were shot dead in South Africa.** On March 21, 1960, police in Sharpeville opened fire on a crowd of Black protesters demonstrating against the pass laws that controlled where Black South Africans could live and move. The Sharpeville massacre led directly to the banning of the African National Congress and the Pan Africanist Congress, and to Nelson Mandela's turn toward armed resistance. Mandela would be imprisoned four years later and would not be free for another twenty-six years after that — not until 1990, when you were twenty-nine years old. You were born three weeks before the event that set in motion a struggle that would not resolve until you were in your thirties.

**Sixty-one days after your birth, a spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union.** On May 1, 1960, an American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft piloted by Francis Gary Powers was downed over Soviet airspace. Eisenhower's administration first denied it was a spy mission. When the Soviets produced the captured pilot and wreckage, the lie collapsed publicly. The Paris summit between Eisenhower and Khrushchev — which had carried real hopes of easing Cold War tensions — fell apart. You were two months old when the possibility of a diplomatic thaw was destroyed by a downed airplane and a failed cover story.

**Television rewrote democratic politics in the year of your birth.** On September 26, 1960, John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon met for the first televised presidential debate in American history. Voters who watched on television thought Kennedy won decisively. Voters who heard on radio thought Nixon had the better of it. The gap between those two groups was a preview of everything that followed: that politics had become, in fundamental ways, a visual medium, and that how a candidate appeared on screen had become as consequential as what the candidate said. This was the world you were entering — one in which the screen was already reshaping the terms of public life.

**Seventeen African nations achieved independence in the year of your birth.** The wave of decolonization that crested in 1960 — Congo, Nigeria, Senegal, Ivory Coast, and a dozen more — rewrote the political map of an entire continent in a single year. The colonial order that had organized global life for a century was dissolving as you took your first breath. The consequences of that dissolution — the post-colonial struggles, the Cold War proxy conflicts fought on African soil, the long work of building nations from borders drawn by European powers — unfolded across your lifetime and are still unfolding now.

---

**The arc of a lifetime.**

You are sixty-six years old, with sixteen February 29ths on record.

Born at the beginning of 1960, the hinge year of the twentieth century's latter half — before the Kennedy assassination, before Vietnam, before the Civil Rights Act, before the moon landing. All of it came during your growing up. Kennedy died when you were three. The Civil Rights Act passed when you were four. Armstrong walked on the moon when you were nine. Watergate consumed the presidency when you were twelve and thirteen. The Iranian Revolution when you were eighteen. The Berlin Wall fell when you were twenty-nine.

The internet arrived in your mid-thirties. The smartphone in your late forties. COVID in your fifty-ninth year.

The world of February 29, 1960 — Cold War at full tension, empires collapsing, a spy plane about to be shot down, apartheid hardening into its most brutal phase — is now history taught to people who weren't born when you turned thirty. You have lived the entire distance from that world to this one, marked by a calendar that only occasionally agrees to acknowledge your birthday.

Sixteen times, the date has been there to meet you. Sixty-six years of everything that happened in between.
